opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the worry wasn't really about the review process or the paperwork. Every big company has some form of approval, and that's understandable. What I was more concerned about was something deeper, which is whether the work could still be truly open.

When you're inside a large industrial lab, especially now, research is increasingly tied to products and competition. There's a natural tension: the company has very good reasons to protect what gives it an edge, but as a researcher, my instinct has always been that the value of a paper comes from other people being able to read it, reproduce it, build on it, and even prove it wrong. If a paper only gives a high-level description, without code, data, or enough detail to replicate, then in some sense it's closer to a technical announcement than to science.

The second worry was timing. The field moves so fast that if publication gets delayed by a few months, the idea might already be out there from someone else, or it might simply be obsolete. So you sometimes feel this pressure: do you rush something out, or do you hold it until it's really solid? I don't think rushing is healthy, but the environment kind of pushes you that way.

And there's a more personal worry too. I care about whether research is driven by curiosity and long-term questions, things like how visual representation should really work, or what the right foundation for multimodal intelligence is, rather than just chasing the next benchmark or the next product milestone. In industry it's very easy for the agenda to slowly drift toward what's urgent rather than what's important. That's part of why I value being in academia as well: it gives me a bit more freedom to work on questions that might not pay off for years, and to share everything openly with the community.

So I'd say my worries weren't about any specific rule. They were about whether the culture of open, curiosity-driven research could survive as AI becomes more and more commercially important. I think that's a question the whole field is facing right now, not just one company.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses openness, publication delays, and research priorities, but does not mention concern that another Google researcher would object to overlap with their research.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, first a small correction, I was actually at FAIR, Meta's research lab, not Google. But the worry you're asking about is real, and I think it's the same at any big lab.

The main thing I worried about was that the work wouldn't be taken seriously on its own merits. When you're at a large company, there's always this suspicion from the community: "Of course it works, they have ten thousand GPUs." So with something like ConvNeXt, I was very anxious that people would say, "This is just scale and tricks, there's nothing new here." Which, honestly, was kind of the point of the paper. We weren't claiming a brilliant new idea. We were asking a very simple question: is the Transformer actually better, or have we just stopped paying attention to ConvNets? The worry was that a "boring" paper, one that doesn't propose a shiny new module, gets dismissed, even if the message matters more than a flashy one.

The second worry was about being wrong in public. Industry papers get a lot of eyes very quickly. If there's a flaw in your experiments, a missing baseline, a leak in the training setup, people will find it within days. And because you're representing a big lab, it's not just your reputation. So we spent an enormous amount of time on fairness of comparison, making sure the training recipe was identical, that we weren't giving one architecture an unfair advantage. That's exhausting, but I think it's the right kind of paranoia.

And then there's a quieter one, which is the fear that the work won't matter. You put a year into something, you release it, and the field just moves on in a different direction. In a company you're also somewhat insulated from the community, so you can lose touch with what people actually care about. I think that's why I've always tried to keep releasing code and models openly, because the reaction from people using it is the only honest signal you get.
